parts.title: Using Satellite Images to Map How Comfortable It Feels Outdoors in Different Neighborhood Types, from Countryside to City, in eThekwini Municipality, South Africa
parts.abstract:
Abstract

We need to keep watching how hot or cold places are, and to understand what that means for the people who live and work there. To do this, we used satellite images to study how comfortable it feels outdoors in different types of neighborhoods, which we call local climate zones. We looked at how this changes as you travel from the countryside into the city in eThekwini Municipality, in KwaZulu-Natal province, South Africa.

To map the neighborhood types, we used images from two satellites, Landsat 8 and Landsat 9. We took pictures taken on different dates and in different colors of light, and we followed a method from the World Urban Database and Access Portal Tools (WUDAPT). We used the satellites' heat readings to work out the land surface temperature, which is how hot the ground, roofs and other surfaces are. To teach the computer what each neighborhood type looks like, and to check how accurate our map was, we drew example areas by hand on Google Earth. We chose these examples using what we learned and the data we collected during a field survey in March 2022, along with maps that already existed.

We sorted the land into neighborhood types with a computer method called a random forest classifier, running in the SAGA GIS mapping software. To find surface temperatures, we used a standard calculation that relies on one heat band (band 10) of the satellite images. We then adjusted these temperatures so they matched the hottest time of day. We used them to work out how comfortable it feels outdoors, using the categories of the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI), a scale that describes how hot or cold conditions feel to the human body. We did this for the extremely low temperatures of the cool season and the extremely high temperatures of the hot season.

Our map of neighborhood types was highly accurate. Overall, 90.1% of the areas we checked were labeled correctly, and the kappa score, a measure of how much better the map does than random guessing, was 0.88. Every pair of neighborhood types could be told apart easily, with a separability score above 1.5.

Built-up areas cover most of the eastern part of the municipality, which shows how much the sea has shaped where people build. On average, the surface was coolest in dense forest, in open low-rise areas (low buildings spread out with open space between them) and in water, in both the cool and the hot seasons. The compact high-rise area (tall buildings packed closely together) was the warmest in both seasons: 36 °C in the hot season and 23 °C in the cool season. The sea sands were among the coolest places in both seasons because they hold a lot of water, thanks to the high water table (the level below which the ground is soaked with water) and their closeness to the ocean.

In the cool season, there was no heat or cold stress anywhere. In the hot season, most areas had moderate to strong heat stress, and some parts of the densely built-up areas had very strong heat stress. Our findings suggest that policies and plans should do more to reduce heat in the areas with strong heat stress during the hot season. City leaders and residents must work together to plan ways of keeping temperatures from reaching extremes, and of reducing the social and economic pressures that come with them.

Plans for how the city grows should think about how they will change temperatures. They should also value protecting neighborhood types that are good at cooling, such as dense forests, and should limit the spread of built-up types that soak up a lot of heat, such as open low-rise. Our study relied mainly on satellite temperatures, with some ground data used to check the results, and this may limit the assessment. Overall, our study offers ideas that can help the world reach its goals for sustainable, climate-smart development.

Keywords: urban climate, heat stress, thermal comfort, remote sensing, WUDAPT, temperature variability
parts.introduction_first:
When temperatures become extreme, either very high or very low, people use more energy to warm or cool their homes and workplaces. This is especially true where people live and where businesses and other activities take place [1–4]. Research has also shown that extreme temperatures can affect how many teenagers are present in schools [5] and can lower how well people work [6]. Warming usually raises the cost of water and increases how much water households and others need [7]. In countries that do not have enough drinking water, heat waves make it more likely that people fall ill from water-borne diseases, because demand for water rises above what is available [8].

Warming is also linked to heat-related illnesses, stress and even death [9,10]. For example, high temperatures can cause or make worse heart and blood vessel diseases, adding to the health burden on top of other illnesses [11]. Studies in the United States have linked heat waves to effects on mental health, including more irritability and depression and more suicides [12,13]. Because temperatures are expected to keep rising, we need to keep watching temperature patterns and understanding what they do to people [8].
parts.introduction_rest:
Satellites give us a way to watch and measure how temperatures change, over small or large areas and over short or long periods of time. For example, the Landsat satellites take pictures in moderate detail, which means each pixel covers a fairly small patch of ground. Their records go back to 1972, so they let us study the land in detail over many years [14]. With these detailed images, we can link patterns of heat across the land to other features of the surface from the same time, such as how the land is used and what covers it, for example buildings, crops or trees [15].

Earlier studies that linked the land surface to land surface temperature mostly used general land-use and land-cover classes. These are broad labels such as "built-up" or "forest". They depend on the judgment of the people who make them, they fit one particular place, and they are not grouped by climate. Maps of neighborhood types made from satellite images work differently. They divide an area into themes that are the same all over the world and are directly tied to climate. This removes the personal judgment and the one-place-fitting problems of the general land-use classes [16]. Each neighborhood type is an area where the surface and the air above it have similar temperatures, and it covers anywhere from hundreds to tens of thousands (10⁴) of square meters [17,18]. Because the types are the same everywhere, using them lets us compare places around the world and understand in depth how patterns of land use and land cover affect heat [16,18]. Neighborhood types also make an important contribution to the World Urban Database and Access Portal Tools (WUDAPT) [19], and they could help plan for sustainable development.

Studies have linked neighborhood types to city temperatures and to heat islands [20–24]. A heat island is a place that is warmer than the land around it. Neighborhood types are also useful for measuring the strength of the urban heat island in a way that is the same everywhere in the world. This is an improvement on the older method, which simply compares the temperature of a city with the temperature of the countryside, a difference that depends on the judgment of the people making it [20,22,25].

Neighborhood types are good for mapping and describing heat, but they have mostly been used for cities. Their possible effect on how heat changes from the countryside into the city has been ignored. Studying this whole range, from the countryside into the city, lets us compare undisturbed, natural surfaces with more built-up areas. Along the way, the land changes by different amounts, from purely rural to purely urban. Rural areas may also offer a more natural landscape to compare against the changed areas nearby, and they may act as a local heat sink, a place that soaks up heat and helps stop heat from building up in the city [26]. By studying how heat changes along this range, we can see how heat stress differs from place to place. We can also find possible ways to reduce heat, and so options for doing so, based on how each neighborhood type is linked to its heat.

In eThekwini Municipality, the land surface changes a great deal from the countryside into the city. There are different kinds of plants, different kinds of buildings and roads, and different amounts of bare soil, and this makes the area worth studying in depth. So far, no maps of neighborhood types cover the whole range from the countryside into the city. In South Africa, only one study, by Sithole and Odindi [27], has looked at how land surface features are linked to changes in heat along this range, in the city of Pietermaritzburg. However, that study used general land-use and land-cover classes, not neighborhood types. Another study in the eThekwini area, by Odindi and colleagues [28], looked at how city green spaces help reduce heat. It also compared how heat behaves in the area with other cities on the southeast coast of South Africa [29].

Even so, eThekwini Municipality has a range from the countryside into the city, with many different neighborhood types and heat conditions that still need to be described. Also, no study in our area has looked at how changes in land surface temperature affect how comfortable it feels outdoors along this range. This matters, because it shows how much comfort outdoors depends on how rural or how urban a place is.

So far, most attention has gone to comfort indoors. This is because people, especially in the developed world, where most of these studies were done, spend much of their time inside [30]. In addition, some outdoor conditions that used to be thought impossible to change can now be controlled [30]. More and more, attention is turning to comfort outdoors. People do important jobs outside, such as repairing roads, collecting rubbish and policing. They also work outdoors in industry and business, such as building roads and running markets, and they play sports and other games [8].

Most studies that use satellite images to measure heat show conditions at a single moment. They are limited by how often the satellite passes over, so they cannot show conditions at the times of day we want. For example, the satellite may pass over at a time that is neither the coolest nor the hottest of the day. This means some data cannot show how comfortable it feels at the moments when temperatures are at their most extreme. These extremes matter for planning, because they show the worst case that people need to be ready for. As far as we know, very few studies have adjusted temperature data to show comfort at times when the satellite is not passing over. In most cases, the satellite's passing time does not match the times of the lowest or highest temperatures, so we need methods to judge comfort at these extremes. Such methods also help us measure how differently neighborhood types behave when temperatures are very low or very high.

For all these reasons, and because residents need to stay comfortable during the extreme temperatures of both the cold and the hot seasons, we used detailed satellite images from the Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 satellites. We had three aims. First, we wanted to map neighborhood types and how land surface temperature varies from the countryside into the city in eThekwini Municipality, South Africa. Second, we wanted to develop a way to estimate heat conditions at the hottest time of day, even when the satellite is not passing over then. Third, we wanted to judge how comfortable it feels outdoors in different neighborhood types, using temperatures adjusted to the right time of day, from the countryside into the city in eThekwini Municipality. In this study, we will map neighborhood types and land surface temperatures, and use them to explain how comfort differs within each neighborhood type and between different types. We will also explore how heat behavior and comfort change from the countryside into the city, using land surface temperature as a stand-in for how comfortable it feels outdoors in eThekwini Municipality.
parts.methods:
2.

Materials and Methods

2.1.

Where We Did the Study: eThekwini Municipality

We studied how neighborhood types (local climate zones) are linked to heat and cold in eThekwini Municipality (Figure 1a), in KwaZulu-Natal Province, South Africa. The green areas (Figure 1b) are made up of neighborhood types with very few buildings, such as farmland, rural homes and forests of different thickness.

The climate is humid and subtropical. Scientists sort climates into groups using the Köppen system [28], and in that system this climate is called Cwa. It has a cool, dry winter from May to October and a hot, wet summer from November to April. Each year, between 500 and 2000 mm of rain falls, usually about 1000 mm on average. In summer, daily temperatures range from 20 to 35 °C, and in winter from 12 to 25 °C. Because temperatures vary so much, both between the cool and hot seasons and within each one, we needed to study how comfortable it feels outdoors in both seasons, to find hot spots and cold spots.

The municipality covers 2212 km² and has 1513 people for every square kilometer. Durban city is the most crowded part, with 35% of the municipality's people [28].

Figure 1

(a) Map of South Africa showing eThekwini Municipality. (b) Landsat satellite image showing how the land surface changes across the municipality and its surroundings. Deep green shows thick plant cover. Grey shows built-up areas, and the brighter the grey, the more densely built the area. In general, more of the land is built up toward the east. Yellow lines show the three transects (straight lines along which we followed the change from countryside to city): Transect 1 (B to A), Transect 2 (C to A) and Transect 3 (D to A).

2.2.

Satellite Data

We downloaded ready-processed images from Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 from the United States Geological Survey (USGS) Earth Explorer website (https://earthexplorer.usgs.gov/, accessed on 16 February 2023). These are called level 1 data, meaning the satellite's raw readings have already been turned into reflectance, which is the share of sunlight the ground reflects in each color of light.

Each pixel in these images covers a square of ground 30 m by 30 m, except for the black-and-white (panchromatic) bands, which show detail down to 15 m. The heat readings come in pixels 100 m across, but we downloaded them already resampled to 30 m. The satellites pass over the same place only every 16 days. This limits how well they can show things that change very quickly, such as patterns that change from hour to hour. Table 1 lists the images we used and the dates they were taken.

No single Landsat image covered the whole study area. So for each date, we joined two neighboring images, from path/row 168/80 and 168/81, into one complete picture of the municipality (Table 1). Path and row are the numbers that mark where on Earth a Landsat image was taken.

For every date, we removed the effect of the air between the ground and the satellite, using a method called dark subtraction [31,32]. This gave us a separate layer for each color of light. We stacked these layers into one file, which we used to map the neighborhood types.

Some neighborhood types, such as those based on plants, change with the seasons. So we needed images from different dates to capture these seasonal changes and help the computer sort the land correctly. We did not use the heat readings to map neighborhood types, because we saved them for working out land surface temperature on the different dates and in the two seasons.

Table 1

The Landsat images we used to map neighborhood types and land surface temperature in eThekwini Municipality.

| Landsat Mission | Path/Row | Date Acquired | Season

| Landsat 8 | 168/80 and 168/81 | 24 January 2022 | Hot wet

| Landsat 8 | 168/80 and 168/81 | 9 February 2022 | Hot wet

| Landsat 8 | 168/80 and 168/81 | 23 March 2022 | Hot wet

| Landsat 8 | 168/80 and 168/81 | 29 March 2022 | Hot wet

| Landsat 9 | 168/80 and 168/81 | 24 May 2022 | Cool dry

| Landsat 9 | 168/80 and 168/81 | 9 June 2022 | Cool dry

| Landsat 8 | 168/80 and 168/81 | 19 July 2022 | Cool dry

| Landsat 8 | 168/80 and 168/81 | 20 August 2022 | Cool dry

2.3.

Example Areas for Teaching the Computer and Checking Accuracy

Table 2 shows pictures of the neighborhood types we found in the study area. We based them on the standard descriptions of neighborhood types in published research [33]. Some types looked alike, so we combined them into the same category. For example, because there are so few buildings in rural areas, it is hard to tell areas with very few buildings apart from areas with low plants.

In other places, different neighborhood types sat side by side within a single 100 m by 100 m pixel of the heat data from Landsat 8 and Landsat 9. This happened mainly in the business district, where tall buildings stood among mid-height and low buildings, on ground covered mostly by hard surfaces such as concrete and asphalt. In these cases, we gave the pixel the label of the neighborhood type that covered the most of it.

To draw our example areas on Google Earth, we used maps of land use and land cover that already existed, such as the European Space Agency's global map, which shows detail down to 10 m. We also used what we learned during a field survey in March 2022. For neighborhood types that cover a large area, we drew at least 20 example areas spread across the study area. This captured the differences within each type and between types, and made the types easier to tell apart.

For each type, we collected example areas using the WUDAPT method [34], at places picked at random around the study area, so that we would capture as much of the variety within each type as possible. We drew a second set of example areas and kept them aside, so we could check the map's accuracy after it was made.

2.4.

Mapping Neighborhood Types and Checking Accuracy

We used the ENVI software to stack the Landsat 8 and 9 images from different dates and colors of light into one file with many layers. This gave each pixel a set of readings, called a spectral signature, that describes how it reflects light. Pixels with similar signatures could then be grouped into the same neighborhood type. Using several dates also let us account for seasonal changes, especially in neighborhood types based on plants and water.

We then used a computer method called a random forest classifier to give each pixel a neighborhood label, guided by our example areas. This is a type of supervised classification, which means the computer learns from examples whose labels we already know. The random forest builds many decision trees, each one trained on a different random sample drawn from the example areas, and then combines their answers [35,36].

We chose the random forest because it gives better results than other methods, such as support vector machines, when the data have many dimensions, like images from several dates and several colors of light [37]. Unlike support vector machines, it also copes better when the example areas are uneven in number or when some data are missing [38]. It has only a few settings to choose, and it can work out which readings matter most, which helps make the map more accurate [39].

We made a neighborhood map of eThekwini and checked it against a separate set of example areas drawn on Google Earth. To check accuracy, we used a confusion matrix, a table that compares the label the computer gave each pixel with its true label from the detailed Google Earth images [32]. We used the separate set of example areas, one drawn for each neighborhood type, for this check.

Following Stefanov et al. [40], Ahmed and Ahmed [41] and Danylo et al. [42], we used this table to work out several measures of accuracy. These were producer accuracy (how many of the true areas of a type were labeled correctly), user accuracy (how many of the areas given a label really belong to that type), overall accuracy (the share of all pixels labeled correctly) and the kappa score.

2.5.

Working Out Land Surface Temperature from Heat Readings

We worked out land surface temperatures for the cool and hot seasons from the heat readings of Landsat 8 and Landsat 9. For each date, we used a standard calculation that relies on one heat band (band 10) [43], because band 11 is not accurate enough. Band 11 is strongly affected by water vapor in the air, and its readings are hard to calibrate, so we used band 10 instead [44].

First, we turned the satellite's raw numbers (digital numbers) into radiance, which is the amount of heat energy reaching the satellite, using Equation (1) [45–47].

(1) Radiance = Gain × DN + Offset

The gain was 0.0003342 for Landsat 8 and 0.00034 for Landsat 9. The offset was the same for both, 0.1. We took these values from the metadata files that come with each image. We then used the radiance to work out the brightness temperature, a first estimate of temperature, using Planck's law for Landsat in Equation (2) [46].

(2) TB = K2 / ln(K1 / Radiance + 1) − 273.16

This calculation assumes that every surface is a perfect blackbody, an ideal object that gives off heat equally well at every temperature, and that all surfaces give off heat equally well. Real surfaces do not. So we added a correction for emissivity, which describes how well a surface gives off heat. We gave each pixel an emissivity value based on the kind of surface it covers. K1 and K2 are fixed numbers: 774.8853 and 1321.0789 for band 10 of Landsat 8, and 799.0284 and 1329.0284 for band 10 of Landsat 9. We took them from the metadata files that come with each image.

We worked out the share of each pixel covered by plants (PV) using Equation (3), and fed it into Equation (4) to get a map of emissivity [48].

(3) PV = [NDVI − NDVIsoil / NDVIvegetation − NDVIsoil]²

(4) Emissivity = 0.004 × PV + 0.986

NDVI is the normalized difference vegetation index, a measure of how green and leafy the plants in a pixel are. NDVIsoil is its value for a pixel of bare soil, and NDVIvegetation is its value for a pixel of plants [48]. Following Subrino et al. [49], we set NDVImin and NDVImax, the values for pure soil and pure plant pixels, to 0.5 and 0.2. We used the emissivity correction to get the land surface temperature in degrees Celsius using Equation (5) [43,45,49].

(5) LST = TB / (1 + λ / (TB × α)) × ln(1 / Emissivity)

λ is the central wavelength of the heat band, which is 10.9 µm for band 10 of Landsat 8 and Landsat 9. α takes the value 1.438 × 10⁻² mK [50].

We used the land surface temperature maps from different dates to show how temperatures changed from month to month in the two seasons. The images came from cloud-free days in both seasons of 2022, so having several dates helped us find the warmest scenes in the hot season and the coolest scenes in the cool season. This helped us study and understand how comfortable it feels outdoors at the hottest and coldest extremes.

2.6.

Adjusting Surface Temperatures to Match the Hottest and Coolest Times of Day

Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 pass over eThekwini at 09:50 in the morning, and they return to the same place only every 16 days. This timing misses the very low temperatures of the night and the very high temperatures of the day. These hours are the extremes of comfort, especially the hottest hours of the day in the hot season and the coolest hours in the cool season. So we needed to adjust the land surface temperatures to show where these extremes happen.

The South African Weather Service gave us temperatures only once a day, which was not detailed enough to study changes over time. So we used temperature readings every 5 minutes from the Ushaka weather station, from the eThekwini Datafeeds website (https://data.ethekwinifews.durban/instrument/stations, accessed on 30 May 2023), which is run by eThekwini Municipality. We chose Ushaka because it was the only station in eThekwini with such frequent temperature readings for the dates we studied. It is also in a hot area, which makes it a good match for studying the hottest extremes.

For each date matching a Landsat image in Table 1, we took the highest temperature of the day (Tmax) and the temperature at 09:50 (T0950hours). The difference between the two told us how much the temperature at Ushaka rose between 09:50 and its peak. We used this difference to estimate how much the land surface temperature rose between 09:50 and its peak. We then added this rise to each scene's land surface temperature to get the day's highest land surface temperature, using Equation (6), which we developed for this purpose.

(6) LSTmax(i) = LST(i) + [Tmax(i) − T0950hours(i)]

Here, LSTmax is the estimated peak land surface temperature for the day, and i stands for each scene. We needed this peak to map temperature and comfort at the extremes, instead of at mid-morning, when the satellites pass over.

We assumed that temperatures across the whole of eThekwini Municipality rise and fall at the same rate as at Ushaka. Ideally, to work out the change in land surface temperature for each neighborhood type accurately, we would need either temperature data with medium-sized pixels or weather stations in each neighborhood type. However, satellite data with medium-sized pixels are not available often enough.

2.7.

Linking Neighborhood Types to Surface Temperature and Comfort in eThekwini

We turned each neighborhood type into a set of points and read off the land surface temperature at each point, using the 'Extract values to points' tool in ArcGIS 10.2 mapping software. We used these values to draw box plots, charts that show the middle and the spread of the temperatures, to compare temperatures between and within neighborhood types. We also used a statistical test called one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) to check whether the average temperatures of the neighborhood types differed by more than chance alone would usually produce. In addition, we looked at the maps to see how temperatures changed from one neighborhood type to another.

Several measures are used to judge how comfortable it feels outdoors: the predicted mean vote (PMV), the predicted equivalent temperature (PET), the outdoor standard equivalent temperature (OUT-SET) and the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI) [11,51,52]. These measures are based on studies in which people and groups were exposed to different levels of stress from their surroundings and from their own bodies' activity [53]. PET and PMV are the most widely used, but measures such as the UTCI are also becoming popular. The UTCI has been found to match closely with the more advanced PMV, OUT-SET and PET, so it is reasonably useful [54].

The UTCI was designed to give standard conditions that work in every climate and do not depend on how much energy a person's body is using. It also works better than other measures in many different climates [11]. The UTCI can directly show what different land surface temperature classes mean for health in cities [25]. Unlike PMV, PET and OUT-SET, the UTCI has simple calculations that have been developed and tested for use with satellite data [25]. For example, Xu et al. [55] used the UTCI to study how outdoor comfort varies in China. Their approach involved complex modeling of relative temperature, pressure, relative humidity and wind speed, and then working out the UTCI (Equation (7)).

(7) UTCI = Tair + f(Windspeed, pressure, Relative humidity, Relative temperature)

Here, Tair is the air temperature.

In another approach, Dutta et al. [25] sorted land surface temperatures into UTCI categories to study outdoor comfort in New Delhi, India. Their approach was simple because the land surface temperature was the only input needed, and it still managed to map how comfort changed from place to place.

Dutta et al. [25] sorted land surface temperatures into 10 UTCI comfort categories: extreme heat stress (above 46 °C), very strong heat stress (38 to 46 °C), strong heat stress (32 to 38 °C), moderate heat stress (26 to 32 °C), no heat or cold stress (9 to 26 °C), slight cold stress (0 to 9 °C), moderate cold stress (−13 to 0 °C), strong cold stress (−27 to −13 °C), very strong cold stress (−40 to −27 °C) and extreme cold stress (below −40 °C). In the same way, the UTCI categories can be used to map comfort in the neighborhood types of eThekwini, from the countryside into the city, because the UTCI works in many climates. We used the peak land surface temperatures (LSTmax) from the warmest scenes in the cool and hot seasons, taken from the data in Table 1, to judge daytime comfort at the extreme temperatures in eThekwini.

2.8.

Possible Sources of Uncertainty in Our Methods

We used the temperature changes at Ushaka to build one adjustment for the whole municipality. In reality, temperature patterns should also differ from place to place, so each place would need its own adjustment. We could not do this, because detailed temperature readings taken on the ground at different places in the area were not available or could not be obtained. The other data we could get were not measured often enough, and some of them had no values at the times when Landsat passed over. Landsat data show enough detail on the ground, but because the satellites pass over only every 16 days, we could not fully study the extremes.

The UTCI involves many complex calculation steps. In this study, we sorted land surface temperatures into UTCI ranges, but actually calculating the UTCI would need other details, such as pressure, relative humidity and wind speed. We had no maps of these extra details, which limited our analysis. We also had no way to check how far the land surface temperatures differ from the UTCI.
parts.results:
3.

Results

3.1.

Our Map of Neighborhood Types in eThekwini

When we looked at the map, we could see that neighborhood types with plants cover most of the northwest and the south of eThekwini Municipality. Built-up types gather toward the eastern edges of the municipality and along the coast (Figure 2). Small patches of built-up types, especially open low-rise, are also scattered across the study area. In some places, densely built-up types such as compact high-rise and large low-rise sit among areas with few buildings.

Figure 2

Map of neighborhood types across eThekwini Municipality, from the countryside into the city.

Beach sand covered only a very small part of the municipality, while low plants covered most of it (Table 3). Water covered more ground than either sand or large low-rise. Of all the built-up types, open low-rise covered the most ground. The densely built-up types (compact low-rise, large low-rise and lightweight low-rise) covered less ground than open low-rise.

Table 3

How much of eThekwini Municipality each neighborhood type covers.

| Neighborhood type | Area (hectares) | Share of the municipality (%)

| Compact high-rise (LCZ 1) | 4650 | 1.82

| Open low-rise (LCZ 6) | 36,032 | 14.09

| Lightweight low-rise (LCZ 7) | 16,941 | 6.63

| Large low-rise (LCZ 8) | 1322 | 0.52

| Dense forest (LCZ A) | 44,822 | 17.53

| Low plants (LCZ D) | 146,529 | 57.32

| Bare soil/sand (LCZ F) | 990 | 0.39

| Water (LCZ G) | 4365 | 1.71

To check how accurate our map was, we compared it with the example areas we had drawn by hand. Overall, 90.1% of the areas we checked were labeled correctly, and the kappa score was 0.88 (Table 4). This showed that we mapped the neighborhood types of eThekwini Municipality with reasonably high accuracy.

We also looked at two more measures for each type. Producer accuracy tells us how many of the real areas of a type we managed to find. User accuracy tells us how many of the areas we labeled as a type really were that type. For producer accuracy, the values ranged from 64% to 99% across the types. For user accuracy, they ranged from 83% to 99.4%.

Producer accuracy was lowest for large low-rise (64.9%) and highest for water (98.8%). User accuracy was lowest for lightweight low-rise (83.3%) and highest for water (99.4%). So water was the type we mapped most accurately, with both producer and user accuracies above 98%. Producer accuracies were lowest (below 75%) for large low-rise and compact high-rise.

Table 4

How accurately the random forest computer method mapped each neighborhood type, using Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 images.

| Neighborhood type | Producer accuracy (%) | User accuracy (%)

| Bare soil/sand | 91.2 | 96.1

| Dense forest | 82.9 | 92.6

| Lightweight low-rise | 96.7 | 83.3

| Low plants | 92.3 | 84.6

| Large low-rise | 64.9 | 93.1

| Compact high-rise | 74.5 | 88.8

| Open low-rise | 74.9 | 88.5

| Water | 98.8 | 99.4

Next, we checked how easily each pair of neighborhood types could be told apart. We used a separability score called the transformed divergence separability index (TDSI). It takes values between 1.5 and 2, and higher values mean two types are easier to separate. Using the example areas we drew and the Landsat images, the types could be told apart very easily.

Among the built-up types, lightweight low-rise and compact high-rise were the hardest pair to separate, with a score of 1.64. Even so, this was still very high, so the two types could still be told apart. For most pairs of types, the score was 2, which shows that the two types in each pair were easy to separate.

3.2.

How Surface Temperature Changed Between the Hot Wet and Cool Dry Seasons in eThekwini

We used satellite images taken in different months, covering both the cool and the hot seasons. Across the whole image, the average surface temperature ranged from 17.7 °C to 28.9 °C. In the cool season, the lowest average was 17.7 °C, from an image taken in August, and the highest was 19.0 °C, from an image taken in July. In the hot season, the averages ranged from 26.2 °C to 28.9 °C, with the highest from an image taken in February and the lowest from one taken in March. The two measurements taken in March were within 0.5 °C of each other. On average, the images from the cool season were at least 7 °C cooler than those from the hot season.

3.4.

How Surface Temperature Varied Across the City in the Cool Dry and Hot Wet Seasons

Figures 3a and 3b show our temperature maps for the hottest time of day on the warmest days of the cool season and the hot season. On both days, temperatures generally rose as you moved east.

On the warmest day of the cool season, temperatures changed little from place to place. Large areas had the same temperature, with a clear split between east and west. On a hot day in the hot season, temperatures varied much more across the city than they did in the cool season (Figure 3b). Figure 3b also shows that the coast was generally cooler than the built-up areas just west of it.

3.5.

Comparing Surface Temperatures Between Neighborhood Types

To compare the average surface temperatures of the different neighborhood types, we used a test called analysis of variance. It checks whether the averages of several groups differ by more than you would expect from normal ups and downs. The test gives a number called the F factor. We compared it with a cut-off value, called the critical F value, that marks when a difference is large enough to count.

In both the cool and the warm seasons, the F factor was greater than the critical value. The p values were also less than 0.05 in every case. This means that if the neighborhood types really had the same average temperature, differences this large would turn up by chance alone less than 5% of the time. So we rejected the starting assumption that all the types had the same average. We concluded that the average surface temperatures of the different neighborhood types were statistically different on the warmest days of both the cool and the hot seasons.

3.6.

How Comfortable It Felt Outdoors in the Cool and Hot Seasons, at Very Cold and Very Hot Temperatures in eThekwini Municipality

On the warmest hour of the cool season, there was no heat or cold stress in the afternoon, and it felt comfortable across most of the municipality. Only a few places in the central east, close to the coast, had moderate heat stress in the cool season (Figure 4a).

On the hottest hour of the day, matching the hottest image, the study area had moderate to very strong heat stress (Figure 4b). Moderate heat stress appeared in the northwest and southwest, in areas with few buildings (mostly countryside) and in areas with no buildings. The northern and northwestern areas with moderate heat stress included Inanda, Amalanga, Mlahlanga, Cibane, Imbozamo, Mgangeni and Indanda. The areas in the south and southwest included Nugwane, Umzinto, Isimahla, Ezimwini, Ogagwini, Mbongolwane and Echobeni.

Strong and very strong heat stress appeared mainly in the east. These places included New Germany, Pinetwown, KwaMashu, Magabeni, Zwelibomvu, Golokodo-Ensimbini, Hammarsdale, Bayhead, Braodway, Siyanda, Glenwood, Prospection Industrial and the Durban Central Business District.

3.7.

How Temperature and Comfort Changed from the Countryside into the City in eThekwini Municipality

To follow the change from countryside to city, we used three transects. A transect is a straight line across the map, and we followed it from a starting point in the countryside to an end point in the city. In the cool season, the city was 2 to 4 °C warmer than the countryside (Figure 5a,c,e). On a day in the hot season, the city was 4 to 6 °C warmer (Figure 5b,d,f).

Along all three transects, surface temperatures went up and down and generally rose as we moved from the countryside into the city. Transect 1 ran from the countryside in the north to the city in the central east. On a hot day, the surface was cool for some distance, then jumped by about 4 °C and stayed around 35 °C all the way to the city end point (Figure 5b). Along Transect 2, from the countryside in the northwest to the city, the temperature changed more gradually on a hot day than along Transect 1. Along Transect 3, from the countryside in the southwest to the city, the change was very gradual (Figure 5f). At the two ends of this transect, the city was 6 °C warmer than the countryside.

Overall, the city was warmer than the countryside more clearly in the hot season than in the cool season. In the cool season, no pixels along Transect 1 or Transect 2 reached moderate heat stress. (A pixel is one small square of the satellite image.) Along Transect 3, fewer than 1% of the pixels reached moderate heat stress.

Figure 5

(a–f): How surface temperature changes from the countryside into the city in eThekwini Municipality. Figure 1 shows the locations of A (the city end point) and B, C, D (the countryside starting points), and the lines of the three transects.

On a hot day in the hot season, the western areas close to the countryside end point had moderate heat stress. As we moved east toward the city end point, the conditions tended to move into the strong and very strong heat stress categories. Along Transect 1, some pixels close to the countryside end point had strong heat stress. No transect had very strong heat stress near the countryside end point. Very strong heat stress became the most common category across the built-up areas in the east.

3.8.

How Comfortable It Felt Outdoors Within and Between Neighborhood Types in the Cool and Hot Seasons

Figure 6 shows the warmest image of the cool season. On that day, the densely built-up types (compact high-rise, lightweight low-rise and large low-rise) were about 1 °C warmer than open low-rise (LCZ 6), where buildings are spread out with open space between them. Open low-rise had almost the same surface temperature as low plants (LCZ D), while dense forest was the coolest. Water was warmer than both open low-rise and dense forest.

In the hot season, lightweight low-rise (LCZ 7) areas had temperatures in a similar range to large low-rise (LCZ 8) areas.

On a hot day in the cool season, almost all pixels in compact high-rise, lightweight low-rise, dense forest, sand and water had no heat or cold stress. However, a few areas (less than 10%) in open low-rise, large low-rise and low plants had moderate heat stress.

On a very hot day in the hot season, compact high-rise was the warmest type and water was the coolest (Figure 7). Open low-rise was the coolest of the built-up types. Sand was among the coolest types, with almost the same temperature as low plants, though warmer than dense forest. Surface temperatures in sand also varied a lot, because some of the sand is on the coast and some is inland. Sand and bare soil were at least 2 °C cooler than the densely built-up types that water cannot soak into (compact high-rise, lightweight low-rise and large low-rise). Unlike in the cool season, large low-rise was warmer than compact low-rise. On a hot day, the types with plants and water were at least 2 °C cooler than the built-up types.

On this very hot day, close to 75% of the pixels in dense forest, 75% in water, 60% in low plants and 40% in sand had moderate heat stress. In contrast, about 35% of lightweight low-rise pixels were below the lowest level of strong heat stress. In general, about 75% of the built-up types had strong to very strong heat stress. Of these, about 20% of compact high-rise, lightweight low-rise and large low-rise areas had very strong heat stress. Open low-rise was not completely spared, as about 10% of its pixels had very strong heat stress.

3.9.

Which Neighborhood Types Had Very Strong Heat Stress

On a hot day, very strong heat stress covered 3255 hectares of the municipality (Table 7). Most of these places were in the east, where homes and businesses are built up. The largest share of these places was in lightweight low-rise (LCZ 7), followed by compact high-rise (LCZ 1). Compact high-rise and large low-rise cover less than 2% of the study area, yet they held the largest share (51.3%) of the places with very strong heat stress.

Open low-rise and low plants, with few or no buildings, cover about 73% of the city. They made up close to 36% of the places with very strong heat stress. Soil/sand and water, which are either covered by water, have a high water table or are close to a body of water, had the smallest share (3%).

4.

Discussion

Our study has shown that local climate zones (types of neighborhoods) can be mapped very accurately from the countryside, through the in-between areas, to the city. We did this by following the WUDAPT method on Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 images taken on different dates and in different colors of light. Several things made the map accurate. The satellite images from Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 are of high quality, and the example areas we drew by hand were representative. The random forest classifier, the computer method we used to sort the land into neighborhood types, is also known to perform very well [37,56,57].

The Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 images we used have high spectral resolution, meaning they record many narrow bands of color, including some our eyes cannot see. They also have a high signal-to-noise ratio, so the real signal stands out clearly from random noise, and high radiometric resolution, so they can pick up small differences in brightness [58–60]. All of this helps when sorting an image into types. Using images from several dates adds information about how things change through the seasons. This combines with the color information to make the types easier to tell apart. Earlier studies that used Landsat and other satellite data have also shown that images from several dates sort land more accurately than a single date [61–66]. The random forest classifier is also known to do better than other methods when it uses data with many different kinds of information [67].

The quality of our example areas can be supported by the separability scores, which were above 1.5. A score close to 2 means that two types can be told apart easily. Our study confirmed that existing land cover maps can be combined with detailed Google Earth images to create these example areas.

The sea shapes how the area develops and how the neighborhood types are arranged. It draws business activity and buildings to the coast, especially near the harbor in our study area. There is less development in the west of the municipality than in the east. As a result, the neighborhood types are arranged differently from place to place, and so are the surface temperatures and the heat stress or comfort.

Lightweight low-rise areas covered a smaller share of the municipality than open low-rise areas. In lightweight low-rise areas, the buildings are packed closely together, are low, and many people live in them. This exposes communities that have little ability to cope with heat to health risks from heat [68,69]. Low-income communities crowd into these areas because land costs a lot per square meter, so they cannot afford roomier homes in open low-rise areas [69].

The bare soil type covered the smallest share of all the types in the municipality. Beach areas could also be set aside for tourism and leisure, because they usually have a higher social and economic value to the municipality. However, these areas have few buildings, such as shops, food outlets and offices, that support tourism, leisure and other businesses.

The low plants type covered the largest share of the municipality. Sutherland et al. [70] also pointed out that the municipality stretches from deep countryside to crowded city, with thinly built countryside dominating the northwest and southwest. Open grasslands inside the built-up types are large enough to be mapped as a separate type from the types around them.

The heat readings from Landsat 8 can be adjusted to map surface temperature and how comfortable it feels outdoors at times other than when the satellite passes overhead. In eThekwini Municipality, the satellite passed overhead in the morning. We wanted to know how comfortable it feels at the hottest time of day, because that is when the risk is greatest. We adjusted the temperatures using readings from a local weather station. This let us map how comfortable it feels during the hottest part of the day on very hot days in both the cool and the hot season. We would not have been able to do this directly with the Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 heat readings. This matters for watching heat stress across a whole region, place by place, using satellite data that is already available.

In the cool dry season, there is little sunlight reaching the ground. So both the built-up types and the types with plants are cool, and the differences between types are small. In the hot season, plants cool their surroundings strongly by giving off water, and how much they cool depends on the type of plant [25]. It is common for surfaces to be warmer in the hot season than in the cool season, and this has been explained by changes over time in how much sunlight reaches the ground [23,36,71,72]. At the same time, neighborhood types that soak up a lot of heat receive strong sunlight, so their surfaces become hot and they differ a lot from other types, especially from types without buildings.

We found that surfaces were hotter in built-up types than in other types, especially in the hot season. Surface temperatures rose as buildings got taller and more crowded, and as more of the surrounding ground was covered by hard surfaces that water cannot soak into. Because of this, compact high-rise areas were the warmest in every season, followed by large low-rise areas. We put the very high surface temperatures in compact high-rise areas down to three things. The buildings soak up a lot of heat. The sky view factor, which describes how much open sky you can see from the ground, is low, so little heat escapes upward. And the buildings slow the wind by friction, which weakens its ability to carry heat away [28,73]. As in large low-rise areas, a very large share of the ground in compact high-rise areas is covered by hard surfaces.

Our study also let us link heat stress to each neighborhood type. This makes it possible to watch and measure the heat risk that comes with each type. The risk can be tied to daytime temperatures and used to build early warning systems that alert people to heat stress risk in different types during hot seasons. Another study [74] predicted that, under future climate change, the whole of eThekwini Municipality would fall into the extreme caution category (32 to 38 °C). Our analysis, by contrast, showed differences between and within neighborhood types across the area, with some places already having very strong heat stress. Capturing these small-scale differences in heat stress matters for choosing actions that fit each place.

Our map of how comfortable it feels outdoors during the day showed that conditions stayed mostly comfortable across the whole municipality during the day in the cool season. In contrast, during a hot afternoon in the hot season, the whole municipality had moderate to very strong heat stress, especially in densely built-up types. In the city of Tel Aviv, Israel, Mandelmilch et al. [73] also found that the amount of sunlight affected how much heat people were exposed to, and that this changed a great deal during the hottest hours of the day. This means that conditions in areas with strong to very strong heat stress are too hot for outdoor activities, and these areas need warnings and action to reduce the heat.

We saw moderate heat stress in the southern and northern areas, which match types without buildings: low plants, dense trees and thinly built countryside. This shows how valuable these types are for reducing heat and as cool places to escape to. It also showed that on a very hot day, even types without buildings feel heat stress, though less than built-up types. Discomfort from heat increased from west to east. This generally points to the effect of changing the land surface, as natural cover is replaced by buildings and other human-made materials that soak up a lot of heat. Wu et al. [75] also saw that countryside temperatures were higher during intense heat. Our findings agree with Lau [76], who notes that differences in the shape and layout of city areas affect not only the local climate but also how hot or cold people feel.

Heat stress can be mapped from the countryside into the city. This helps us understand that different places need different responses, and shows how important countryside and in-between areas are for reducing heat in cities. The temperature difference between countryside and city was larger on an extremely hot day in the hot season than on an extremely cool day. The small difference in the cool season could be because plants and soil hold little water in the dry season, which weakens the cooling effect of surfaces. Some low plants also dry out in the dry season. In Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, dry surfaces were found to conduct heat about as well as city areas [77]. In Kuwait, thin plant cover was found to behave much like built-up areas in terms of heat [78]. Our findings also agree with Lee et al. [79], who found higher temperatures in city areas than in countryside areas in Xuzhou.

According to McCarthy et al. [80], the large amount of heat given off by human activity in cities also helps make them hotter than the countryside. In the same way, industry and emissions from sources such as vehicles dominate the built-up east of eThekwini Municipality, and this may also add to the temperature difference with the countryside. Changes in the countryside–city temperature difference with the seasons have also been seen in Beijing, where the difference was large in spring, summer and autumn and small in winter [2]. We carried out our hot-season analysis on an extremely hot day, which makes the differences larger because countryside and city areas soak up heat at different rates. Wu et al. [75] also found that the countryside–city temperature difference was larger during intense heat in Taipei in Taiwan and Yilan in Japan. In our study, the difference between countryside and city could reach about 6 °C, while in Rotterdam in the Netherlands it even reached 10 °C. These differences show that countryside areas provide a natural service that is very valuable for reducing heat when temperatures become extremely high [81,82].

Our findings showed that heat stress depends on how an area has developed. The way built-up types and types with plants are arranged has a strong effect on how much heat stress people feel, and on how much they benefit from types that soak up little heat. Climate change policies and plans have mostly focused on water and farming, but paying attention to how temperatures change and to heat stress has proved to be just as important. At the same time, plans need to differ from place to place and fit how heat behaves in each area, because a one-size-fits-all approach would put the places most at risk at a disadvantage. For example, in eThekwini Municipality, action to reduce heat proved more necessary in densely built-up areas where many people live.

Our findings could help provincial and city leaders find the areas where they should assess plans to adapt to heat and to reduce it. They also showed that leaders need to find the money and resources to help communities in areas most at risk from heat to cope with extremes. In addition, our method showed that eThekwini Municipality needs more instruments that measure how comfortable it feels outdoors, checked often, to make observations and models more accurate. Finally, policies and plans for protecting plants and water areas need to be strengthened, because they have proved very valuable for reducing heat in the municipality. This should include encouraging greening efforts, such as growing plants on roofs.
